question_text: Choose the correctly spelled word to complete the sentence: 'The city __ voted unanimously to pass the ordinance.'

hint_ladder.title: Orient Yourself
hint_ladder.text: This is a classic case of two words that sound almost identical but have completely different jobs. The blank needs to be the subject of the verb 'voted' — so it has to be a noun that names a group of people who can vote.

hint_ladder.title: The Simple Rule
hint_ladder.text: Think of 'council' as the group that meets in a hall to make decisions. Think of 'counsel' as the advice you get from a lawyer or a trusted friend. One is a body of people; the other is guidance or the act of giving it.

hint_ladder.title: Apply the Rule Here
hint_ladder.text: The sentence is about a city body that voted. That's a group of people, not advice. So you need the word that means an assembly. Also, check the grammar: 'counciled' isn't a real word, and 'counsels' would be the wrong form for this spot.

hint_ladder.title: Almost There
hint_ladder.text: Only one option is a noun that means a group of people who meet to govern or make decisions. That's 'council.' The others either mean advice, don't exist, or are the wrong verb form.

A.text: Correct. 'Council' is exactly the word you need here — it's a noun that refers to an assembly of people gathered to discuss or decide on matters. In this sentence, the city council is the group doing the voting.

B.text: This is a very common mix-up. 'Counsel' can be a noun meaning advice or a verb meaning to give advice. It's easy to see why someone would pick it — it sounds just like 'council.' But a city body that votes is always a 'council,' not 'counsel.' Think of it this way: you seek counsel from a lawyer, but you elect a council to represent you.

C.text: This one might look plausible if you're trying to make 'council' into a verb, but it's not a real word in standard English. 'Council' is a noun, and you can't just add '-ed' to it. The trap here is thinking you need a past-tense verb, but the sentence already has 'voted' — the blank needs a noun.

D.text: This is a clever trap. 'Counsels' is a real word — it's the third-person singular form of the verb 'to counsel' (he counsels) or the plural of the noun 'counsel' (pieces of advice). But neither works here. The sentence needs a singular noun for a group, and the correct plural of 'council' is 'councils,' not 'counsels.'

next_time_rule: Here's a simple trick that will never fail you: 'Council' has a 'c' like in 'committee' — both are groups of people. 'Counsel' has an 's' like in 'suggest' — both are about giving advice. When you see a sentence about a group voting, deciding, or meeting, your brain should immediately reach for 'council.'
deconstruct_text: Let's walk through this together. The sentence says 'The city ___ voted unanimously.' The word that goes in the blank is the subject of the verb 'voted,' so it has to be a noun that names a group of people who can vote. Now look at your options. Option A, 'council,' is a noun that means exactly that — an assembly of people convened for governance or deliberation. That fits perfectly. Option B, 'counsel,' is a common homophone that means advice or the act of giving advice. A city council can vote; a piece of counsel cannot. Option C, 'counciled,' isn't a standard English word at all — someone might have tried to turn the noun 'council' into a verb, but that's not how English works. Option D, 'counsels,' is either the verb form of 'counsel' or its plural noun form, but neither refers to a voting body. The correct plural of 'council' is 'councils.' So only option A works. The mental trick here is simple: whenever you see a sentence about a group that meets, decides, or votes, think 'council' — the word with the 'c' for 'committee.' Whenever you see a sentence about advice or guidance, think 'counsel' — the word with the 's' for 'suggest.'
